newsitem.title: BELARUS: FEATURE - Economists see hint of thaw in unreformed Belarus.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Economists see hint of thaw in unreformed Belarus.

text.p: Hardline President Alexander Lukashenko has had three months to reshape his rule in Belarus since he won sweeping powers in a referendum and economists whisper cautiously that they see signs of a thaw.
"Two swallows don't make a spring...but I detect some signs of a change of heart," said a senior monetary official.
While opposition activists talk of a "Minsk spring" and a repeat of protests which led to battles with police last April, Lukashenko has made a small but meaningful change in policy.

The former farm boss seems to have decided to introduce a free currency regime, if gradually, and economists say visits by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank could restart a reform process which had gone into reverse.
And with January monthly inflation at 13.3 percent, the 42-year-old's go-slow approach could be coming unstuck.
NO PROMISES OF CASH YET, BUT MUCH POTENTIAL
The IMF did not discuss new funds to replace a $300 million standby credit it froze a year ago during what it described as a "fact-finding mission" in February.
But the Bank said it would offer a $30 to $40 million loan to support small business development and sign a loan memorandum soon if Belarus renewed an IMF macroeconomic reform programme.
It would be good news after a year without credits, a poll denounced as fraudulent and endless messages from European bodies telling Lukashenko to reform and respect human rights.
"I would consider 1996 to be a lost year for Belarus. It is falling further and further behind," the monetary official said.
"Countries don't disappear, they just wallow down there and make do. I think it's an incredible pity to see that happening at the doors of western Europe."
But a well-educated population, good geographical position and a reasonable infrastructure inherited from the Soviet Union could make Belarus a candidate for recovery.
"They could make a living just out of transit trade between Russia and Western Europe," the monetary official said.
"They're going to have to make it the way countries do when they don't have natural resources which is to have a very open economy, the fewer controls the better."
AN ECONOMY THAT'S GROWING
Despite all the gloom, gross domestic product rose 2.6 percent and industrial output by 3.2 percent in 1996.

Otherwise, the record makes painful reading, with receipts from profit taxes down 40 percent, shipments to warehouses down 19 percent, inventories up, loss-making enterprises up, and only a handful of a planned 567 enterprises privatised.
"If all that is happening then the increase in output was sort of fake. It's all being financed through bank credit and arrears. That's not a sustainable situation," said one economist.
The question on every reformer's lips in Belarus is how long Minsk can resist tough monetary controls being endured by its neighbours in Russia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine.

"You can (resist) for years and years and years if you're willing to accept the political cost of being backward all the time. Then the politicians are going to have to explain why everybody else is doing so well," the economist warned.
ROUBLE RATE STARTS TO SWIM
Until recently the central bank, by order of Lukashenko, fixed the rate of the Belarussian rouble at about 30 percent more than the rate on interbank markets outside the country.
But new central bank chief Gennady Aleinikov, who says his main goal is to make the rouble convertible, has introduced a market rate.
Many curbs still remain on trade of the rouble, nicknamed the zaitchik after the hare depicted on a one-rouble note which went out of circulation long ago.

Only strategic importers of much-needed energy supplies can buy dollars freely on the Minsk exchange, where the rouble drifted from the old fixed rate of 22,050 rouble per dollar to 22,710 by late February.
It is still well above the Moscow interbank rate of 30,000.
Foreign businesses, not to mention Belarussians who cannot buy dollars for foreign trips or just for peace of mind, complain bitterly about the gap.
Some Belarussians queue all day outside currency exchange points. "Are you selling? Are you selling?" they whisper.
Warren Grawemeyer of Coca Cola Amatil said the currency regime was the biggest problem faced by foreign businesses.
"We've been promised a level playing field, but actually we have a 30 percent disadvantage. We are holding lots of roubles," he told Reuters, speaking before the rate was freed.
PASSIVE BELARUSSIANS

Analysts say that geo-political factors, history and Belarus' reputation for being "passive" have helped create a situation where Lukashenko's authoritarian approach could take root and create what is in essence a command economy.
Economic problems include a dearth of raw materials and an artificial manufacturing base geared to meet Soviet demands.
The population is older because it was a retirement destination, which analysts say helped Lukashenko win the 1996 referendum, disbanding parliament and rewriting the constitution so easily.
But opposition members and young people struggling to get businesses going are increasingly critical of Lukashenko, saying he has deliberately slowed up reforms to hold on to power.

"Patient? What do you mean, be patient?" said Vadim, a taxi-driver in his early 30s, snorting at the suggestion that reforms might eventually push his monthly salary back up from the $15 he earned in January to $400 he earned 18 months ago.
"If this had happened anywhere but Belarus, there would have been bloodshed by now, like in Belgrade. Give me a gun and I'll shoot him myself. For nothing," he added, smiling grimly.
Market traders joined the crowds at a recent opposition rally, enraged that Lukashenko had renationalised Minsk's central market, forcing thousands out of work.
"This is a new phenomenon because businesspeople are taking part," said Lyudmila Gryaznova, an economist from the old parliament which is still recognised by the European parliament.
"They have realised their freedoms are being restricted too," she said against a backdrop of 2,000 protesters with banners reading: "Long live Belarus in the centre of Europe".
The traders had joined forces with nationalists who hate Lukashenko's policy of forming a union with Russia.
"We didn't want to take part in politics. But we don't know how we'll feed our families tomorrow!" one trader yelled.
RUSSIA AND ENERGY SUPPLIES COULD PLAY A DECISIVE ROLE
While the absence of foreign credits and a noisy opposition could influence Lukashenko, the biggest factor is Moscow. "It all depends what Russia does," one economist said.
Lukashenko is seeking some kind of union with Russia, but that would be impossible without extensive economic reform.
Moreover, Belarus owes Russia's Gazprom gas monopoly $40 million. Its oil refineries, dependent on Russian supplies, have come close to a halt because of the currency crunch.
"In the end it's Gazprom that could decide it. It's a big game, and it's all about whether Russia can outmanoeuvre Luukashenko and force him to liberalise," said a Minsk-based Western economist.
